About this document

This document provides the teaching content for Visual Arts Years 11 of the
New Zealand Curriculum.

Progress and assessment information for Visual Arts Years 11 is still in development.
Once that is completed, Visual Arts Years 11 is proposed to be made by the Minister
of Education as a National Curriculum Statement under section 90(1)(a) of the
Education and Training Act 2020.

It is proposed that, once made and published in the New Zealand Gazette, schools
who offer Visual Arts Years 11 will be required to start using it in Year 11 from
1 January 2028.

This document will be replaced with the official version made under the Act and
published in the New Zealand Gazette once that has occurred.




Visual Arts | Years 11 | October 2026                                                   Page 2

Te toi whakairo, ka ihiihi, ka wehiwehi, ka   Artistic excellence makes the world sit up in
      Purpose statement                                                             aweawe te ao katoa.                           wonder.




  In Visual Arts, students are taught how artistic ideas, materials, processes, and
  visual language are used to create authentic artworks. Students learn to
  investigate, develop, and refine ideas in response to personal intentions and
  contexts, applying visual arts concepts across painting, design, photography,
  printmaking, and sculpture. Through creative exploration, students use materials,
  methods, and conventions to communicate ideas effectively.

Students are taught key visual arts concepts and practices and how artists
communicate ideas through visual language, symbols, and creative processes. They
examine a range of contexts, including local, Toi Māori, Pacific, and global, to
understand how artworks reflect different perspectives and meanings.

Visual Arts provides students with the knowledge and practices to investigate,
analyse, evaluate, and apply understanding through artmaking. This disciplinary
knowledge supports students to create original and resolved visual outcomes while
developing confidence in communicating ideas, interpreting the world around them,
and responding thoughtfully to diverse contexts and viewpoints.

As students progress through Year 11, they are taught to develop technical,
conceptual, and contextual knowledge to create, analyse, and evaluate artworks and
artmaking practices. This enables them to make informed artistic decisions and
communicate ideas effectively through visual and written forms. They work with
increasing confidence to refine and realise artistic ideas that are ethical, culturally
responsive, and informed by contemporary artistic and technological contexts.

  Visual Arts leads to pathways in the arts, design, media, and creative industries,
  including fine arts, photography, illustration, animation, visual communication,
  creative technologies, and related cultural sectors.

 Disciplinary Writing

 Focus: the use of writing to reflect the ways in which knowledge is organised, analysed, and communicated within the discipline.
 In Visual Arts, students use explicitly taught disciplinary writing to analyse established practice and communicate the creative ideas, processes, intentions, and meanings in their
 own and others’ artwork.

 Responsible use of artificial intelligence
 Artificial intelligence (AI) can support learning, research, inquiry, and creative processes, but it may also introduce bias, inaccuracies, ethical concerns, and issues relating to
 ownership. AI should enhance, not replace, critical or creative thinking, source evaluation, subject knowledge, or students’ own analysis and decision-making. Responsible AI use
 emphasises the importance of exercising independent judgement, drawing on credible sources, verifying information, being transparent about AI use, considering diverse
 perspectives, and developing independent thinking.

 Drawing

  Drawing is an essential component of Visual Art and underpins all visual arts fields.
  Drawing is a foundational and ongoing process.
  Drawing can be a resolved artwork.
  Drawing includes, but is not limited to, line, texture, mark-making, tonal shading, colour, gesture, stippling, hatching, contour, thumbnail sketches, compositional planning, value
   studies, preparatory studies, planning, diagrams, maquettes, contact sheets.
  A series of drawing studies using a range of 2D media is expected to support the generation of ideas in each field studied (e.g. observational drawings, compositional studies).
